This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a high-dimensional Schrödinger equation. By assuming the ground state's real-valued symmetry, we derive an upper limit on the generalization error in the norm and entire weight space for a pair of mirror-symmetric networks. This bound depends solely on the chemical potential and desired accuracy, independent of the system's dimension. Furthermore, we provide a proof-of-concept implementation that achieves the predicted generalization performance. The findings are validated through numerical experiments on a multi-particle model in one-dimensional space. The results show that the proposed approach successfully estimates the generalizable output over the entire weight space, even in high dimensions. The output's accuracy is found to be highly dependent on the network's architecture, particularly the number of neurons. The findings suggest that larger networks may not necessarily enhance generalization performance. The study's analytical generalization guarantee is expected to contribute significantly to the development of efficient and reliable numerical methods for solving high-dimensional partial differential equations. Artificial neural networks, the inspiration behind deep learning, consist of neurons with variable receptive fields that respond to specific stimuli. To overcome these limitations, we propose an enhanced neural model, where the output is a continuous value rather than a binary decision, by incorporating an inhibitory component that suppresses neuron activation when input signals are excessive. This modification enables neurons to more accurately represent their surroundings, thereby improving overall network performance. Our experimental results demonstrate that this enhanced model achieves superior accuracy and robustness in image classification tasks, as evidenced by its ability to handle noisy inputs and ambiguous patterns. Furthermore, we have successfully applied this model to the challenging problem of out-of-distribution data detection, where it exhibits impressive performance. This paper explores the concept of steganography in the context of text encoding, focusing on a novel approach that employs LSTMs. By applying this method, we can embed a hidden message within a seemingly innocuous piece of text, which can only be deciphered by those aware of the specific encryption key. Our research builds upon the existing text steganography framework proposed by Hill, first described in 1886. In contrast to the existing image-based steganography paradigm, widely studied in the field, our study delves into the challenges and potential solutions of text steganography. Specifically, we investigate the optimal character selection for hiding and reveal the relationship between the chosen character's conditional probability and the actual character's occurrence rate. Furthermore, we introduce an LSTM model as a potential solution to enhance the steganographic text's quality. Our experiments involve collecting and processing a large dataset of 8,000 pairs from online news sources, which serves as the foundation for our training and testing phases. Our findings demonstrate that the LSTM model significantly outperforms the baseline approach, achieving a higher PS and NP scores while maintaining an acceptable AR score. In addition, we examine the effectiveness of our approach in resisting various types of attacks. Ultimately, we assess the potential applications of our method in real-world scenarios. Replay-based methods in reinforcement learning exploit past experiences to speed up training, but the impact often depends on the quality of the chosen experiences. Current techniques focus on incorporating diversity to prevent past successes from dominating learning, but don't address another issue: the variance of returns from past actions, which can mislead the policy improvement process. High variance significantly hinders the effectiveness of experience replay. To address this, we introduce a new approach, Variance Diminishing Experience Replay (VDER), which selectively chooses experiences based on both diversity and return variance. VDER outperforms leading methods in various robotic tasks and achieves faster convergence, ultimately resulting in better task outcomes. Our proposed approach is versatile and can be integrated with existing replay-based methods to enhance their efficacy. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/kuo-yi-weng/vder.

Pretraining methods based on autoregressive language models like BERT have shown remarkable success in natural language processing tasks.  However, these models face limitations due to their autoregressive nature, which hinders their ability to model bidirectional contexts.  We present XLNet, a fully contextual language model that overcomes these limitations by factorizing the probability distribution and incorporating additional contextual information through augmented data generation.  By combining the strengths of autoregressive and autoregressive-decoders models, XLNet achieves improved performance on a wide range of tasks while reducing memory usage by half compared to BERT-like models.  We demonstrate XLNet's superiority through extensive experiments on 20 different NLP tasks, including benchmark tests on GLUE and SemEval-2010-2, and show that it outperforms the current state-of-the-art on various tasks.  The source code and pre-trained models for XLNet are available at https://github.com/zhanghanghuihalide/XLNet.  Our results suggest that XLNet can serve as a robust foundation for NLP tasks and further advances the state-of-the-art in language modeling.  Moreover, our analysis sheds light on the importance of augmented data generation in fully contextual language modeling.  We anticipate that our findings will inspire future research on this topic. The influence of weak intermolecular forces is increasingly acknowledged in organic chemistry, yet applying theoretical models to accurately predict their behavior in electric fields remains a significant challenge. To address this issue, we have conducted a comprehensive study using high-level quantum chemistry methods to analyze the electric dipole moment, polarizability, and second harmonic polarizability of 19 molecules in the S66 dataset, which are then used to calculate non-bonded interaction energies between these molecules in response to an electric field. Our results demonstrate that these properties can be reliably predicted through a single-point approach, enabling the accurate calculation of non-bonded interaction energies in electric fields. Furthermore, we have developed a model that combines the first three electric dipole hyperpolarizability components to describe the electric field-dependent non-bonded interaction energy, which is found to be in good agreement with the results from high-level quantum chemistry methods. This approach is expected to be particularly valuable for the simulation and understanding of organic molecules in external electric fields. A visual system utilizing a 3D geometric map can efficiently navigate complex environments by leveraging a pre-constructed, spatially-organized representation of the surroundings. However, relying solely on this map for navigation can be problematic in dynamic or newly-acquired environments. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative approach that combines 3D geometric mapping with visual relocalization techniques. By integrating a global geometric framework with a local appearance-based matching system, our approach ensures accurate navigation in environments with changing visual characteristics. To optimize performance, we have developed a novel neural network that generates spatially-organized feature representations, which significantly enhance the accuracy of our relocalization results. Experimental evaluations on both simulated and real-world datasets have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy. Notably, our approach has achieved a localization error rate of 0.11 meters on the challenging KITTI dataset, representing a 2.5-fold improvement over the previous best result. The corresponding source code is available for public access on the GitHub platform.

Document ranking is a crucial task in information retrieval, but it's often plagued by label noise, which causes problems for traditional loss functions. To address this issue, we're proposing a new approach that involves training a ranking model using a representative sample of documents, which we've dubbed "bag sampling." By using a group-level loss function, our method mitigates the negative effects of label noise and improves the model's robustness. In addition, we've developed a technique to estimate the noise rate of a specific field, which we've incorporated into our bag sampling framework. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods, achieving significant gains in robustness and accuracy. Moreover, we've found that our bag sampling technique can be applied to other information retrieval tasks, such as dense retrieval. In many real-world applications of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), we often encounter a common challenge: working with limited labeled data. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel approach called Informative Pseudo-Tagging (IPT), which effectively utilizes unlabelled data to generate high-quality pseudo-labels for GNNs. By incorporating a temporal component, IPT leverages the historical evolution of node features to create informative pseudo-labels, which are then refined through a iterative process. Experimental results across three public datasets demonstrate that IPT outperforms existing methods of generating pseudo-labels, ultimately leading to superior performance on downstream tasks. Notably, IPT achieves comparable results to supervised baselines even with as few as 1% labeled data. The implementation of IPT is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyuyang2018/Informative-Pseudo-Tagging.

Researchers at the AWAKE experiment are employing a self-modulating proton bunch to produce a short, highly energetic electron beam through a process known as laser-driven electron acceleration. By injecting electrons into the center of a 10-meter-long, 1.3-meter-diameter plasma column, they are able to observe unique physics and investigate innovative acceleration techniques. A key consideration in this research is the Betatron radiation emitted by the electrons as they oscillate within the plasma, which can be used to monitor the quality of the electron beam. A simulation model has been developed to analyze the Betatron radiation emitted by the electrons, taking into account their spatial and temporal distributions within the plasma. This model has been applied to AWAKE Run 2 data, which includes 40 MeV proton bunches and a 10 TW laser pulse. Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a widely used algorithm for optimizing convex objectives, but its effectiveness can be significantly impacted by noisy gradient estimates. While the standard SGD method with a high enough step size can theoretically achieve optimal convergence rates in the presence of noise, this often comes at the cost of large steps that can lead to unstable behavior and slow convergence on smooth objectives. To address this issue, we propose a new class of adaptive SGD methods that not only account for noise levels but also take into consideration the objective's smoothness. By leveraging this information, these methods can adjust their step size to achieve faster convergence rates in a variety of scenarios, including cases where the noise characteristics and objective properties change over time. Our research provides a foundation for the development of future adaptive SGD methods that can effectively handle noisy gradient estimates and varying objective properties. nonlinear, time-dependent coupling between oscillators. We demonstrate that
their behavior can be accurately described by a simple model based on the
concept of synchronization. In systems with this new type of coupling, two

synchrony is similar to traditional synchronization, but weak synchrony gives
rise to periodic changes between in-phase and out-of-phase states. This
phenomenon is observed in both autonomous and driven systems. We also explore
the transition from strong to weak synchrony, as well as the potential to use
this effect for energy harvesting. Theoretical findings are supported by a
range of numerical simulations. The research includes an experimental study
examining the dynamics of two pendulums with variable coupling strength. The
results reveal the presence of weak synchrony in these systems, which is
further analyzed using the proposed model. Overall, this research provides
insights into the complex behavior of the studied systems and opens up new
possibilities for harnessing energy from the pendulums' motion. Finally, we
discuss potential applications of the discovered effects in various fields.

Asynchronous parallel evolutionary algorithms have become a preferred approach for efficiently solving complex optimization problems.  However, their performance is often hindered by evaluation time disparities among individuals.  This issue can be particularly problematic in parallel multi-objective evolution where parent selection is typically used to ensure diversity in the population.  This paper introduces a novel parent selection strategy that utilizes the frequency of selection as a key factor to mitigate evaluation time bias.  By favoring less frequently selected individuals, the proposed method aims to reduce the impact of evaluation time disparities and improve population diversity.  Experimental evaluations conducted on a range of test functions demonstrate that the proposed strategy outperforms existing methods, particularly in high parallelization scenarios.  Furthermore, the study shows that the proposed strategy is effective across different parallelization environments and is suitable for use in asynchronous parallel multi-objective evolution.  Overall, the results suggest that the proposed frequency-based parent selection strategy is a valuable contribution to the field.  The source code is available for public use at https://github.com/fernandoamorim/frequency-based-parent-selection. Deep learning-based object detectors have achieved impressive performance in various applications, yet their reliability in critical domains such as self-driving cars and medical imaging remains uncertain. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called BayesOD, which integrates a Bayesian neural network for object detectors. By incorporating a prior distribution on model parameters, BayesOD quantifies the prediction uncertainty and enhances model interpretability. In addition, our method assumes that object labels are drawn from a Poisson distribution, which enables the estimation of uncertainty and object count accuracy. Experimental evaluations on multiple public datasets demonstrate that BayesOD significantly improves uncertainty estimation for object detection tasks. Notably, our method demonstrates a 6.8% mAP increase in uncertainty estimation on the NuImage dataset and a 3.2% mAP improvement on the MS-COCO dataset compared to the standard evaluation metric. The source code for BayesOD is publicly available on GitHub. With this contribution, we aim to promote transparent and accountable object detection models. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the importance of model priors in estimating uncertainty and offers insights for future research in this area. A critical factor in understanding and diagnosing hippocampal abnormalities is precise segmentation. This process can be challenging due to the hippocampus's small size and irregular shape within MRI images, which often results in partial volume effects. To address this issue, we developed a multiple input convolutional neural network (MCNN) that utilizes three distinct hippocampus views from 3D MRI scans. This approach enables the MCNN to account for partial volume effects and irregular hippocampus shapes by combining information from the three views. Our study demonstrates that the MCNN outperforms single-input CNNs by achieving higher Dice coefficients and reduced Hausdorff distance values. Furthermore, we found that the MCNN's performance is robust to different hippocampus orientations. This finding suggests that the MCNN can be applied to a wide range of hippocampus views, making it a versatile tool for various clinical studies. To validate the MCNN's performance, we applied it to two datasets from epilepsy and Alzheimer’s disorder studies and obtained promising results. This study showcases the effectiveness of the MCNN in accurately segmenting hippocampal regions from MRI scans. Additionally, we provide a detailed computational analysis of the MCNN's performance and discuss its potential applications in clinical research. This study proposes a method to improve relation extraction by utilizing knowledge graph link prediction techniques to generate candidate relationships. These candidates are then filtered using contextual clues from the input text, and an adapted attention mechanism is applied to select the most relevant information for classification. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in relation extraction. Additionally, the paper examines the underlying principles of this technique and suggests a potential explanation: relation extraction models trained with knowledge graph completion can generate context-specific hints that aid in relation identification. This hypothesis is supported by two case studies, which reveal that models trained with knowledge graph completion tend to rely on less obvious contextual cues, whereas those without this training rely more heavily on explicit context markers. This novel connection highlights a promising avenue for integrating these two tasks and could lead to more effective relation extraction in the future. In complex cooperative systems, developing adaptable team behavior is challenging due to the unpredictable nature of teammates' actions. To address this issue, we present a novel framework based on off-policy reinforcement learning that relies on a unique transfer empowerment metric to assess the impact of an agent's policy on its partners' behavior. By promoting behaviors that increase teammates' freedom of action, this framework enables agents to effectively respond to their partners' actions and achieve better cooperation outcomes. Through simulations in various cooperative tasks, we demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves higher cooperation rewards compared to alternative methods, including those that rely on mutual information between an agent's and partner's behavior. Additionally, we showcase the robustness of our framework in scenarios where partner behavior is unknown. Our approach provides a novel mechanism for modeling the interdependence of agents' behavior within cooperative systems and can be applied to a wide range of cooperative tasks. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/ku-robotics/transfer_empowerment.

By incorporating a self-supervised pre-training stage that simulates diverse environments and viewpoints, the network becomes resistant to changes in lighting and camera perspectives. A new method, called detector-free local attribute matching with transformers (LoFTR), addresses these limitations by leveraging the self-attention mechanism in transformers to match local features without relying on pre-trained detectors. Instead, LoFTR uses a simple yet efficient network to directly match local features across different images. By doing so, it achieves high accuracy at a much faster speed than state-of-the-art methods. In particular, it can process video at 30 frames per second, even on a single GPU. Furthermore, it outperforms other methods on benchmark datasets such as KITTI and 7Scenes by a significant margin. Notably, it also achieves high accuracy on a new, large-scale dataset called TUM-3D, which features indoor and outdoor scenes with complex backgrounds. Overall, LoFTR's simplicity and speed make it an attractive option for real-world applications. A code repository and dataset for TUM-3D are available online.

To address this issue, we investigate techniques for simplifying these models when only partial information is available. We propose two methods for removing unnecessary model components: one that uses a cost-minimization approach to identify key parameters, and another that employs a similarity measure to filter out irrelevant model elements. We evaluate these methods on a simplified model of a quadcopter system, comparing their performance against a baseline that uses complete data. The results show that our methods can effectively reduce model complexity while maintaining accurate predictions, and even outperform the baseline in some cases by achieving better performance with fewer model components. Additionally, we explore the challenges of adapting these methods to complex systems and discuss potential solutions. In display advertising, real-world bidding competitions are driven by revenue maximization, often influenced by an upper budget limit per ad slot. To address this, we developed a novel bidding strategy called ARB, tailored to online auction systems requiring instant decision-making. By treating the remaining budget as a time-varying risk level, ARB adapts to changing cost-per-action and adjusts its risk aversion based on the probability of running out of budget. Through theoretical analysis, we established the conditions under which ARB's expected return converges to the optimal Monte-Carlo Upper Confidence Bound performance. Furthermore, we conducted experiments on public datasets, demonstrating that ARB surpasses state-of-the-art methods like Thompson sampling and Bayesian Intrinsically Motivated Prior Exploration in both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Notably, ARB's performance is achieved with significantly fewer Monte-Carlo simulations than these benchmark methods. The findings are further validated by a case study on a real-world dataset. The proposed ARB strategy is now available as an open-source Python library on GitHub. The code can be easily integrated into existing commercial bidding systems to enhance their performance. We introduce a novel reward learning approach that utilizes visually identified cluster rankings to expedite the process. This method leverages the capability of deep neural networks to accurately recognize objects and assign corresponding labels, even in the absence of complete annotation. By focusing on group rankings rather than individual object labels, we can efficiently obtain high-quality annotations. Our approach is then combined with a ranking-based reward learning method, which iteratively refines both the visual and reward models in tandem. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over existing reward learning techniques. Notably, our approach achieves comparable performance to reward shaping using comprehensive annotations but with significantly less time and resource requirements. For instance, it achieves a 0.88 average AUC score with only 10 hours of annotation, whereas traditional reward shaping necessitates 120 hours. Moreover, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art reward learning methods by 0.10 AUC score on average. This method's effectiveness is further validated through experiments on multiple datasets, including the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Celeb datasets. This study proposes a novel approach to interpretability by framing it as a learning process for human learners and quantifying it as the cognitive complexity of the required learning process. By applying this framework, we can evaluate an algorithm's interpretability using its cognitive complexity score (CCS). We developed a human-learning-based model (HLM) to illustrate this concept, which simulates human learning to perform a task using an ML algorithm's explanations. By testing HLM with three ML models, we found that its CCS correlates with human evaluators' subjective assessments of an algorithm's interpretability. This research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding interpretability as a learning process and offers a practical method for measuring it. Furthermore, we found that CCS can be used to identify and compare the strengths and limitations of various algorithms and even anticipate potential errors. Our findings suggest that interpretability is not solely determined by an algorithm's technical capabilities but also depends on how easily it can be understood by humans. The COMET-ATOMIC 2020 dataset is an expansion of the original COMET dataset, featuring 1.5 million atomic facts that build upon 200 million relationship frames. This dataset enhancement enables researchers to assess advancements in identifying relationship frames and subframes, as well as to analyze subframe prediction as a distinct problem. Our results demonstrate that even with the limited information provided by atomic predicates, high-quality subframes can still be accurately predicted. We also introduce a new evaluation metric that accounts for the order of predicted subframes and their parent predicates, as well as a baseline model that leverages symbolic reasoning to predict subframes. Our analysis of the performance differences between neural networks and symbolic reasoning suggests that the two approaches are tackling different aspects of the subframe prediction problem. Ultimately, we find that combining the predictions of both methods yields the best results, achieving a 10% relative improvement over the baseline model. Our code and data are available for download at https://github.com/allenai/comet-atomic-2020.

Firstly, they need to efficiently manage and allocate resources to unreserved virtual machines (VMs) while ensuring high system utilization. Secondly, they must effectively schedule and provision VMs with reserved CPU resources for guaranteed quality of service. To address these issues, we propose an innovative load distribution approach called prepartitioning (prepartition) that dynamically allocates reserved and unreserved VMs to hosts using a reserved VM-centric method. By leveraging prepartition, we can prevent overcommitment of reserved VMs and minimize waste of allocated resources. Domain adaptation is a significant challenge in adapting a model to a target domain with limited or no target data availability. The'source data distribution' refers to the distribution of the source domain's data, which is often unidentifiable in practice. To address this, we propose a new method called Semi-Supervised Hypothesis Shift (SHS), which assumes that a hypothesis with a similar distribution shift can effectively adapt a model to the target domain using semi-supervised target data. SHS achieves this by first identifying a new hypothesis with a similar distribution shift to the target domain and then using semi-supervised target data to retrain the model. We demonstrate that SHS can be applied to various distribution shift hypotheses, including non-linear hypothesis shifts. We also show that SHS can be used to address the challenge of adapting a model to the test domain in transfer learning scenarios. Experimental results show that SHS significantly outperforms existing methods in adapting a model to the target domain in various domain adaptation tasks. Answer set programming offers a clear syntax for modeling and both evaluating and explaining the reasons behind computed solutions. However, the current paradigm for explanation is limited to examining individual, recursively applied grounds of the input program, which restricts the scope of analysis to the level of basic atoms. This paper presents a more comprehensive approach to explanation that enables the examination of higher-level structures within the model, such as query expressions and their components. To facilitate this, we introduce a novel mechanism for grounding any part of the model, which allows for the generation of all relevant grounds, including those not explicitly listed in the program. This mechanism is then used to develop an explanation language that encompasses not just the original grounds, but also their derived extensions. To demonstrate its utility, we have implemented a system called ExpLab that provides an interactive environment for exploring and analyzing the various levels of model structure. ExpLab's capabilities are showcased through a series of example scenarios. In this research, we address the challenge of action detection from video data, focusing on identifying the key frames where a specific action occurs. Given the sheer scale of video data and the labor-intensive process of manual annotation, we propose a weakly-supervised approach to action detection. This method involves training a model using action video clips and corresponding labels without frame-by-frame annotation. Instead, we leverage the entire video clip as a single entity to identify action-specific frames. Our approach builds upon the principle that action video clips contain graph information, where nodes represent frames and edges signify spatial and temporal connections. By applying graph convolutional networks to these connections, we enable the model to learn context and pinpoint action-related frames within video clips. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, yielding impressive performance on JHMDB and 50Salads datasets. Notably, we achieve comparable results to fully-supervised methods, with a significant reduction in required video clips for training. This breakthrough enables the model to accurately detect action instances using fewer training samples. Our code is available for public access at https://github.com/chenyilong85/spot-what-counts.

To translate ASR output into written text, inverse text normalization (ITN) is employed, with a major hurdle being the conversion of numbers and quantities. Despite the effectiveness of machine learning-based ITN, data-driven methods excel in quality but struggle with limited training data coverage. We address this limitation by developing a unique pre-processing technique that expands the scope of ITN data and significantly boosts model performance, with the best results showing an improvement of 4.4% in the BLEU-4 metric compared to the previous best outcome. This breakthrough is achieved through the integration of two key methods: a sequence-to-sequence based word-replacement approach that generates new ITN examples by replacing numbers and quantities with word alternatives, and a text infilling method that fills in missing numbers and quantities in ITN data. Furthermore, we introduce a data selection strategy that optimizes the quality of the generated data for better ITN performance. We also adapt a state-of-the-art ITN model to handle the expanded dataset, with the outcome demonstrating the value of data augmentation in improving ITN quality. The proposed method is extensively evaluated on the ATIS, SNLI, and TAC 2019 datasets, with the results showing consistent improvements across all datasets. identifying the most important words or phrases from a given text. Current NLP models

considering the impact of model pruning and knowledge distillation methods. Our findings
suggest that these methods can be employed to optimize NLP models for IoT devices, leading
to improved efficiency without compromising accuracy. To facilitate future research,

resource for the community. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/

This research presents an unsupervised speech synthesis system that achieves high-quality outcomes with minimal reliance on annotated data. The approach is grounded in the idea of using a pre-trained, widely-distributed language model as a universal language decoder for speech. To bridge the gap between text and speech, a novel duration model is introduced, and a data generation technique is developed to produce synthetic training data for the system. The results indicate that the proposed method surpasses existing unsupervised speech synthesis techniques in terms of voice quality and articulation accuracy, with the added benefit of requiring significantly fewer parameters and exhibiting greater scalability. Notably, the system demonstrates exceptional performance even when the training data consists of brief, sentence-level audio clips. The emotional undertones conveyed through language are pivotal in understanding the overall sentiment expressed, yet current approaches often disregard this emotional aspect. To address this, we suggest a novel framework for aspect-based sentiment analysis that explicitly learns emotional nuances. Our method involves a two-stage training process: initially, we employ a supervised contrastive learning technique to capture the underlying emotional patterns in words and their relationships, followed by fine-tuning on the specific task of aspect-based sentiment analysis using word embeddings rich in emotional content. Experimental results on six prominent datasets demonstrate that our approach surpasses the current state-of-the-art performance. Notably, the effectiveness of our method is most pronounced in cases where the dataset contains a high level of emotional expression. These pre-trained models can be utilized in other NLP tasks to capture implicit emotional content. object. This integrated structure, called the Joint Parsing Object (JPO), is built

structure, followed by a semantic parser that re-ranks the syntactic tree to
produce the most likely JPO. This JPO is then used to inform the parsing of
subsequent sentences, resulting in improved accuracy on various datasets,

explanatory parsing trees, and even the syntactic tree itself, through a

decoding algorithm that efficiently searches for the optimal JPOs. Our method is

To prevent optimization path oscillations, we apply a specific interval restriction that limits sampling to a predetermined range. Our method's efficiency stems from the use of the same mean and standard deviation for all neurons in a layer, eliminating the need for layer-wise computations typically required in such algorithms. stability. This study investigates the impact of various loss functions on the
performance of the MobilenetV3 model, using the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets.

generalize, with certain losses resulting in superior generalization when
combined with different batch normalization techniques. Notably, the MobilenetV3 model
performs best when paired with the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss and batch
normalization with moving mean and variance. Our findings also highlight the
advantages of incorporating a small amount of random noise during training, which
can improve the model's resistance to perturbations and generalization to unseen
data. Overall, this study provides valuable insights for practitioners to make
informed decisions when selecting a loss function for their network architecture.

which can be used to analytically determine the loss function that minimizes the 
difference between the model's gradients and those of a reference model. This 
method enables the identification of loss function parameters that result in 
similar gradient profiles, thereby facilitating the transfer of knowledge between 
different models. The gradient surgery method can be applied to both supervised and 
unsupervised settings and is expected to be a useful tool for researchers and 
practitioners seeking to understand the impact of loss functions on model

We develop a new class of holographic error correction codes, known as hyper-invariant MERAs, which maintain their tensor product structure even after multiple rounds of erasure. By applying the quantum approximate Markov inflation principle, we establish a lower bound on the bond dimensions of hyper-invariant MERAs in terms of the physical Hamiltonian parameters. This leads to a specific condition for achieving perfect quantum numerical renormalization group results, as well as insights into the behavior of certain systems at critical points. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between hyper-invariant MERAs and stabilizer codes, and outline a method for constructing new code families within the holographic tensor network framework. This research contributes to our understanding of approximate projective entanglement purification and may have implications for the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing algorithms. Light field data, which is available in every point of a scene, is difficult to capture and store due to its high dimensionality. However, it is also hard to process, as conventional image compression techniques fail to account for the scene's depth and parallax. To overcome this challenge, we propose a new model that combines a conventional image compression method with a parallax-aware model, which predicts the disparity map of the scene. Our model, which is based on a neural network, can be trained on synthetic data and provides accurate results on real-world datasets without the need for additional processing. By using this model, we can apply conventional image compression methods more effectively, resulting in better results. Our experiments show that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of compression ratio and subjective quality. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexander-kuhnt/light_field_compression.

By combining the strengths of interactive and non-interactive models, we develop a hybrid approach that outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of recall while also improving computational efficiency. The integration of these models through a simple ranking strategy demonstrates promising results, with the hybrid model achieving a 10% increase in recall over monolingual English systems and a 2x reduction in query processing time compared to the top CLIR solution. We suggest a quantum computing strategy that combines digital and analog techniques to efficiently simulate complex fermionic systems on quantum computers with limited qubit resources. By leveraging the concept of fermionic modes, where the quantum simulator adapts to the unique characteristics of the system, such as its Fock space structure and Hamiltonian, we can efficiently represent the quantum properties of fermionic modes using a smaller number of qubits. Specifically, we propose an analog-digital approach that utilizes variational quantum evolution to simulate the system's dynamics, where the fermionic modes are represented by qutrits and simulated using digital methods, and the fermionic operators are represented by photonic modes and simulated using analog methods. Our approach allows for efficient simulation of complex fermionic systems using a smaller number of qutrits and photonic modes, and we demonstrate its feasibility using a 3-mode system as an example. Furthermore, we investigate the scalability of our approach and demonstrate that it can efficiently simulate complex systems such as the Hubbard model and the Anderson impurity model using current quantum simulators. Our results demonstrate the potential of our approach to efficiently simulate complex fermionic systems on current quantum computers. Additionally, we discuss the potential applications of our approach in quantum chemistry and condensed matter physics. Our work provides a roadmap for efficiently simulating complex fermionic systems on current quantum computers. In a multitasking allocation problem with shared processing, a principal assigns tasks to multiple agents, who can either complete the tasks on their own or outsource them to other agents at a cost, while also considering the risk of subcontracted tasks being rejected. The principal aims to determine the optimal task distribution and cost-sharing mechanism that incentivize agents to complete all assigned tasks at the lowest overall cost. However, existing knowledge on single-task allocation and cost-sharing mechanisms does not directly apply to this problem, as task difficulties vary and are unknown to the principal. To address this challenge, we propose a new class of mechanisms that achieve the desired outcomes in this shared processing context. These mechanisms work by first categorizing tasks into distinct types and establishing a fixed pricing system for each type, which in turn determines the principal's and agent subutility functions. By leveraging the properties of type-additive and cross-section-monotone mechanisms, we show that such mechanisms can achieve desirable outcomes, including individual rationality, ex-post efficiency, and ex-post individual rationality, while also providing a general framework for applying existing single-task allocation mechanisms to the shared processing context. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed mechanisms can be implemented through simple and truthful lotteries over single-task allocation mechanisms. To illustrate the practical applications of our results, we provide examples of mechanisms that achieve better outcomes than previously known benchmarks in specific scenarios. Finally, we discuss the potential extensions of our work to more complex settings, such as when agents have private preferences over their own tasks. By addressing these issues, we can further improve the efficiency and fairness of task allocation and cost-sharing in the shared processing context. Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are limited in several ways. For instance, they often overlook the factual accuracy of summaries, ignore the redundancy in the original text included in the summary, and are not adaptable to varying summary lengths. Furthermore, existing metrics are often biased towards specific characteristics of human-written summaries. To overcome these limitations, we present SummScore, a novel assessment method that relies on Cross-Encoder models to evaluate summary quality. Our approach involves breaking down the summary evaluation process into three distinct components: (a) a fact-checking system to verify the factual accuracy of summaries; (b) a bias-adjustment mechanism to fine-tune the model's performance according to human-written summary characteristics; (c) a length-normalization technique to standardize summary lengths for comparison. Experimental results demonstrate SummScore's superiority over existing metrics in terms of correlation with human evaluation across various summarization datasets. Additionally, we release an open-source tool for SummScore and make available a high-quality dataset of annotated summaries for further research purposes. This research investigates the recovery of complex-valued sparse signals from a special type of non-adaptively collected data, known as quadratic measurements. For a specific class of quadratic matrices defined by low-rank patterns, we develop a theoretical framework that examines the number of measurements required to accurately reconstruct the signal. Our findings demonstrate that for these matrices, the required number of measurements grows linearly with the signal's dimension, provided that the signal's spectral norm is sufficiently limited. Furthermore, we develop a practical algorithm that produces an approximate solution with an error rate closely tied to the inverse of the number of measurements. Our results are supported by numerical experiments that demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in various scenarios. Notably, we observe that for a broad class of signals featuring heavy-tailed distributions, the algorithm's performance surpasses that of adapted methods, such as basis pursuit. Additionally, we derive a lower bound on the number of measurements required for general quadratic matrices and show that our proposed method approaches this bound as the measurement count increases. Finally, we explore the applicability of our findings to a range of real-world applications, including the recovery of complex-valued signals from phaseless imaging data and the estimation of time-varying frequency coefficients. Our numerical results indicate that our proposed method excels in these applications, particularly when the signal's properties are characterized by heavy tails. For instance, we observe that our method significantly outperforms adapted methods in the context of speech signal estimation. Our research also reveals that our method is highly competitive in the context of magnetic resonance imaging, where it is able to recover detailed images from a relatively small number of measurements. Overall, our findings demonstrate the potential of quadratic measurements for accurately reconstructing complex-valued sparse signals, and we anticipate that our research will contribute positively to the development of novel signal processing techniques. We introduce BEVFusion, a straightforward yet powerful lidar-camera fusion framework, by leveraging BEVFusion to predict 3D bounding boxes and their corresponding 2D references in the camera coordinate system. Traditional lidar-camera fusion methods often rely on complex fusion techniques, such as feature matching and projection. In contrast, BEVFusion adopts a straightforward approach by directly utilizing lidar-derived 3D bounding box predictions as input, along with their projected 2D references in the camera coordinate system. This simplified framework enables the development of more effective and efficient lidar-camera fusion methods. Furthermore, BEVFusion incorporates a novel 3D bounding box prediction loss, which combines both 3D and 2D reference losses to facilitate accurate 3D bounding box predictions. Experimental evaluations on the Waymo Open Dataset and KITTI dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of BEVFusion, with results indicating that it outperforms other lidar-camera fusion methods across multiple metrics. Notably, BEVFusion achieves a 4.0 m 3D IoU on the Waymo Open Dataset, surpassing the benchmark set by the top-performing model in the competition. Code implementation and dataset resources for BEVFusion are available on the author's GitHub page.

Deep learning has achieved significant success in numerous fields, and its applications in control theory are becoming increasingly prominent. However, deep learning methods often rely on overparameterization, which allows these models to effectively learn and generalize from limited training data. This paper aims to provide a framework for validating deep learning control models through the lens of adaptive control theory. By leveraging the universal approximation theorem and constructing a specific loss function, we establish conditions to ensure that learned neural networks can be adapted into stable, continuous control systems. The main contributions of this paper involve establishing a method for validating neural networks, which is demonstrated through a numerical example showcasing its practical applications. The research also highlights potential avenues for future investigation. The methods and findings presented in this paper are expected to have a positive impact on the development of neural networks for control systems. Clustering is a fundamental data analysis technique used to compactly represent sets of mixed-categorical and continuous features. However, existing methods fall short when dealing with datasets that have overlapping cluster structures. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach called Functorial Hierarchical Clustering, which builds upon a theoretical framework to create more robust and interpretable clustering models. Our method can be applied to both continuous and mixed-type features, and it's available in the R language through the 'funclust' package. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing it to existing state-of-the-art methods on synthetic and real-world datasets. The results show that our approach outperforms others in terms of accuracy and scalability, and it's particularly well-suited for large datasets due to its efficient memory usage. Furthermore, we visualize the overlapping cluster structures using interactive visualizations to facilitate interpretation. Overall, our approach provides a new way to model complex data structures and it's a valuable tool for data analysts to uncover hidden patterns in their data. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance in both synthetic and real-world datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. This study builds on the findings of a previous paper by Guzman and Mizuhara, who classified Nichols algebras over finite Weyl groups, with the exception of $W(B_n)$, $W_D_n$ and $W_F_4$. In this paper, we fill the remaining gaps in their classification results. Similar to their work, ours relies heavily on the classification of graded Lie superalgebras developed by Huang, Zhang, Guo and Niu. In addition, we utilize the existing classification of infinitesimal Hopf algebras over Weyl groups, as established by Bruegmann, Guzman and Zhang. Combining these classifications with the findings of Guzman and Mizuhara yields a comprehensive classification of Nichols algebras over traditional finite Weyl groups. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the generic irreducible Nichols algebras over $W(B_n)$ and $W_D_n$ are isomorphic to the Chevalley Lie superalgebra $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2n)$. In contrast, the corresponding Lie superalgebra for $W_F_4$ remains unidentified. In addition, we identify a generic Nichols algebra over $W(B_4)$, which is isomorphic to the Lie superalgebra $\mathfrak{su}(2|3)$. In the case of finite Weyl groups, the generic irreducible Nichols algebras are either isomorphic to $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2n)$ or possess a Hopf algebra structure with a diagonal projection. In the process of our research, we also identified a generic Nichols algebra over $W(B_3)$, which is isomorphic to the Lie superalgebra $\mathfrak{osp}(1|6)$. This study examines how humans and image classification models react to extreme image distortions. We discovered that models are significantly impacted by these distortions, both positive and negative, whereas humans are more resilient. Notably, both humans and models respond similarly to moderate distortions, but differently to severe ones. This finding has significant implications for evaluating machine learning models using naturalistic image transformations. We also introduce a new metric called "reliability of shift" to measure how consistently models perform across various distorted versions of the same image, and apply it to analyze the effects of different transformation types on models. Our research reveals that severe image distortions can provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of machine learning models, and can be utilized in future evaluations to assess their performance in more realistic scenarios. We hope this research will contribute to the development of more accurate and reliable machine learning models for image classification. Designing observers for complex dynamic systems is crucial in epidemiology, where it's often necessary to estimate disease transmission parameters and infection rates. However, the nonlinearity of these processes, combined with the lack of complete state information, poses significant challenges. This study addresses these issues in the context of two widely used epidemiological models: the SIS model with proportional transmission and the SIS model with frequency-dependent transmission. By adapting an extended Kalman filter for nonlinear systems, we propose a state observer that leverages incomplete state measurements to estimate the infection rates and other critical parameters of these models. Our approach is supported by theoretical convergence proof and validated through simulation examples. The proposed method demonstrates the ability to estimate infection rates and other parameters for both model types, showcasing its potential as a valuable tool in epidemiology. Furthermore, we explore the application of this observer to a more complex model with frequency-dependent transmission, highlighting its adaptability to various epidemiological models. The proposed observer is expected to contribute significantly to the estimation of disease transmission parameters, which is essential for designing effective control strategies against infectious diseases. Previous research has highlighted the prevalence of misused cryptography in software development, 
but it focused solely on code samples within code repositories, failing to account for real-world attacks 
influenced by human error, misapplication of best practices, and social factors. To explore the broader issue, 
we conducted a comprehensive study of cryptocurrency misuse in widely-used Python libraries, encompassing

being repeated across multiple issues. Furthermore, we found that the majority of issues with cryptocurrency misuse 
are not addressed, and when they are, the resolution often fails to rectify the underlying problem. Our research also 
investigated the root causes of cryptocurrency misuse, including the interplay between social factors, code complexity, 
and the presence of security-related issues. Ultimately, we propose a set of guidelines for developers, maintainers, and 
security researchers to enhance awareness and address cryptocurrency misuse. Our findings and recommendations can

The proliferation of geotagged social media data has made it an invaluable resource for understanding urban environments. However, the sheer volume and diversity of this data pose significant challenges for processing and analyzing it effectively. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework called VALUE, which leverages user voting patterns to identify relevant locations and assign relevant tags to urban areas. By aggregating social media posts into distinct locations and allowing users to assign tags to these locations, VALUE capitalizes on the collective wisdom of social media users to produce high-quality urban mapping results. Empirical evaluations conducted on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in producing accurate results. Furthermore, VALUE's output aligns well with crowdsourced tagging platforms like OpenStreetMap, thereby facilitating seamless integration of the results into existing urban mapping frameworks. With its ability to handle large-scale data analysis, VALUE offers a scalable solution for urban planning and management applications. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved significant success in image recognition tasks by utilizing isotropic convolutional operators. However, these operators may not capture anisotropic patterns found in some natural images. To address this limitation, we propose Direction Convolutional Networks (DCNs), which incorporate a novel convolutional operator that considers both local and directional contexts. By applying this operator in CNNs, DCNs can effectively recognize anisotropic patterns and improve overall performance. Our results demonstrate that DCNs outperform traditional CNNs on a range of synthetic and real-world image datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet. Moreover, DCNs exhibit improved robustness against common image corruptions and adversarial attacks. To facilitate further research, we have made our code and pre-trained models available for public access. 

Key findings include:

- DCNs surpass state-of-the-art performance on MNIST and CIFAR-10/100 benchmarks.
- DCNs show superior performance on Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet compared to traditional CNNs.
- DCNs exhibit improved robustness against various types of noise and adversarial attacks.
- DCNs achieve state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet with robustness against noise and adversarial attacks.

Our research indicates that DCNs can effectively recognize anisotropic patterns and improve overall performance in image recognition tasks. To facilitate further research, we have made our code and pre-trained models available for public access.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) models, comprising multiple neural networks
trained on different input modalities and output spaces, are often underutilized
due to inefficient communication between component networks. To address this issue,
we investigate the application of lightweight, efficient neural networks
designed for feature sharing, such as ResNets, to the MIMO framework. By leveraging
shared feature extractors, our approach enhances model performance and reduces
computational requirements. Empirical evaluations on the Hatefuls dataset
demonstrate the efficacy of this strategy, yielding improved performance and
significantly reduced inference costs without sacrificing accuracy. The proposed
method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/akshayR7/feature-sharing-in-mimo.

This study explores the hyperbolic characteristics of K3 surfaces with complex Picard forms within their period matrices. Specifically, we establish that a K3 surface with a Picard form as 2κ up to integer scaling, where κ is a positive integer less than or equal to the Minkowski discriminant, possesses a Siegel disk of bounded radius. Conversely, we demonstrate that for any given positive integer κ less than half of the Minkowski discriminant's square root, there exists a K3 surface with a Picard form scaled by κ and a period matrix within the Siegel upper half-plane, whose corresponding Siegel disk is bounded. Moreover, we show that for any given period matrix of a K3 surface, there exists a K3 surface with an identical period matrix for its Siegel upper half-plane counterpart. Additionally, we derive an upper limit for the Minkowski discriminant based on the K3 surface's complex Picard form and period matrix. This research also examines the hyperbolic characteristics of K3 surfaces with complex periods derived from Fermat's Last Theorem solutions. The adaptive spectral Koopman method has shown great potential in solving complex dynamical systems, but its current implementation has been limited by the high computational cost associated with kernel-based and matrix-based approaches. These findings are expected to pave the way for the application of the adaptive spectral Koopman method in real-world systems. This paper presents a novel approach to reduce positional bias in LiDAR point cloud alignment using deep neural networks. Conventional methods rely on a single scan matching pose, which can lead to significant errors and poor convergence rates due to positional bias. To address this issue, we have developed a deep neural network filter that leverages a sequence of pose estimates to eliminate or minimize their associated biases. The proposed method is based on a dynamic model that simulates the movement of a sensor through sequential scan poses, allowing it to identify and mitigate positional bias. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves a 20% reduction in average error and 40% reduction in failure rates compared to state-of-the-art methods across a range of challenging indoor and outdoor datasets. Furthermore, the approach exhibits a high degree of robustness, with a 90% success rate on the KITTI dataset even when faced with the most severe positional bias. In the field of deep learning, researchers have successfully applied various architectures to solve the problem of modulation classification. However, these systems can be vulnerable to attacks that manipulate the input, such as adversarial examples. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called the blend generative adversarial network (BGAN) that can enhance the resiliency of modulation classification systems against such attacks. The BGAN consists of multiple generative models with different architectures, and its discriminator is designed to combine the features of multiple gradient estimators through a blend process. By integrating multiple gradient estimators, the BGAN's adversarial training process becomes more stable and efficient. Furthermore, we utilize the adversarial training process to fine-tune the feature representation of the classification model, which can improve its resiliency against adversarial examples. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed BGAN can significantly improve the classification accuracy of modulation classification systems under attack, and its training process can also enhance the resiliency of the classification model itself. Additionally, we investigate the impact of different network architectures and training methods on the performance of the BGAN. The findings of this study can provide valuable insights for researchers working on adversarial robustness in communication signal processing. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuyang1989/blend-GAN.

Our research indicates that by leveraging the structure of preference data, we can develop more effective contextual preference learning models. This work refines the end-to-end Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture by incorporating a Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) retriever for text data. Building on existing research that demonstrated the effectiveness of pre-training RAG models and DPR retrievers separately, our study investigates whether combining these components leads to enhanced question-answering capabilities. This research contributes to the ongoing exploration of the interplay between passage retrieval and generation components in the RAG architecture, with implications for the development of more efficient and effective question-answering systems. In the realm of multimedia search, text-to-image retrieval has garnered significant attention in recent years. This research addresses the challenging task of text-image retrieval, specifically text-image matching, with the goal of retrieving an image clip in response to a spoken question. This task is complex due to spoken questions often lacking clear visual answers, making it difficult to pinpoint the correct image clip. To tackle this problem, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel transformer-based model that shifts and selects image tokens to retrieve the most relevant image clips. TS2-Net achieves this by employing a multi-stage architecture, incorporating a token shifting module to align image tokens with spoken questions, a token selection module to filter and retrieve relevant image clips, and a multi-modal matching module to enhance the model's understanding of visual and linguistic cues. To further improve performance, we also develop a data augmentation technique, which involves generating pseudo questions to augment the model's training data. Our approach demonstrates superior performance on widely-used benchmarks, surpassing the state-of-the-art by a substantial margin. The accompanying code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/whwu2018/TS2-Net. unstructured formats like text, images, and sequences. Unlike existing methods
focusing on non-convex optimisation-based solutions, Spartan employs a
differentiable framework with a unique sparse output representation. This
representation leverages a continuous, discrete-valued vector to indicate
output sparsity, enabling a straightforward optimisation using regularised
transportation theory. Spartan's efficiency lies in its simplified cost
function, reduced memory requirements, and fast numerical propagation. In
experiments, Spartan surpasses existing methods in producing sparse outputs
while maintaining high quality and achieving faster training times. Notably,
Spartan's success in generating concise yet informative image descriptions
marks a significant improvement over current state-of-the-art methods. The code
is publicly available at https://github.com/SebastianMontag/Spartan.

Understanding complex relationships within vast knowledge bases relies heavily on visual representation, but current approaches often oversimplify by focusing on hierarchical structures, neglecting non-hierarchical connections. To address this, we've developed OntoPlot, a novel visualization that showcases both types of relationships, allowing users to explore and understand the rich associations within large ontologies without the limitations of a purely hierarchical perspective. OntoPlot's design incorporates a two-part layout, featuring a hierarchical tree on one side and a network-based visualization on the other, that highlights non-hierarchical connections, with click-and-drag interactions enabling users to navigate between related concepts across both visualizations. Through its intuitive design, OntoPlot facilitates exploration and understanding of large ontologies, as demonstrated in our case study involving the OpenCyc ontology. The tool is available for open access at https://github.com/vis4ml/onto-plot.

Our research delves into the Soret effect in gases composed of deformable molecules whose internal structures are influenced by temperature. By employing molecular dynamics simulations, we investigated the Soret coefficients for helium and nitrogen, focusing on their thermal expansion and kinetic viscoelasticity properties. The results revealed that nitrogen's Soret coefficient is nearly twice that of helium, a finding attributed to nitrogen's internal degrees of freedom. To validate this, we conducted a series of simulations using a simplified model, where we simulated a gas composed of two-atom molecules with varying bond lengths. The results showed that when the light atom is smaller compared to the heavy atom, the thermal expansion property dominates the Soret effect, whereas when the heavy atom is smaller, the kinetic viscoelasticity property becomes the primary contributor. These findings suggest that the Soret effect in gases can be significantly influenced by the internal structures of deformable molecules. Moreover, we discovered that the Soret effect can be controlled by adjusting the size difference between the atoms within the molecules. The results of our study provide valuable insights into the design of materials with thermomolecular flow behavior. This study evaluates the performance of several efficient Transformer models for automated essay assessment in a standardized testing context. The evaluation is based on their ability to accurately assess essays across various proficiency levels and identify duplicate submissions. In addition, the paper examines the computational efficiency of these models in terms of training time and power consumption, considering their potential use on various hardware platforms. The findings suggest that the models tested, including TinyBERT, MobileBERT, and EfficientBERT, exhibit comparable performance to the conventional BERT model in automated essay assessment. However, the models vary significantly in terms of computational efficiency, with TinyBERT and MobileBERT achieving a 4-6 times speedup in training and inference phases, albeit at the cost of slightly reduced accuracy. The research highlights the importance of balancing model performance and efficiency in automated essay assessment and suggests that the latter could be a key factor in real-world deployment. The findings also emphasize the need for further optimization techniques to improve the accuracy of efficient Transformer models. The research code and data are publicly available on GitHub. High-recall domain adaptation for pedestrian detection is crucial for surveillance systems, requiring significant tolerance of false positives to detect as many target objects as possible, even if they are non-pedestrian. However, this approach often results in a substantial number of false positives, making efficient processing and post-processing essential. To address this challenge, we introduce the Box Re-Ranking (BRR) method, which employs a ranking network to identify high-confidence pedestrian boxes while suppressing non-pedestrian boxes. BRR is an unsupervised method that is adaptable to various scenarios. To improve its performance, we also develop a Box Re-Ranking Loss (BRL) and a novel metric called the Pedestrian-Box Embedding Distance (PBED). The PBED metric measures the similarity between positive and negative pedestrian boxes, while the BRL loss minimizes the inter-class similarity of non-pedestrian and pedestrian boxes. The BRR method is evaluated on the Citypersons dataset and the Caltech dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The source code is available on GitHub. This can be particularly useful in fields such as epidemiology and astronomy, where the detection of events is often subject to limitations. Finally, we discuss the potential connections between this process and the concept of Pareto principle, also known as the 80-20 rule. This principle suggests that a significant portion of effects in a system are often caused by a small number of underlying causes. By applying the multiplicative stochastic process, we can gain insights into the distribution of these causes and their impact on observed phenomena. Overall, this work highlights the utility of multiplicative stochastic processes in modeling complex systems and extracting meaningful information from empirical data. Moreover, it emphasizes the importance of considering the limitations of measurement and data collection when analyzing such systems. By doing so, we can gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms and their implications for real-world applications. Ultimately, this work contributes to the development of new methods for analyzing and interpreting stochastic processes in various fields. We also employ a combination of a global and local feature matching strategy to ensure that the manipulated images are visually coherent. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in manipulating fashion images while maintaining accurate visual identity verification. Moreover, our approach outperforms existing baselines in fashion image retrieval tasks. This research presents a comprehensive framework for fashion image retrieval, encompassing three key components: visual identity manipulation, feature-level attribute adjustment, and fashion image retrieval. Estimating depth from a single light field image is a complex task, particularly due to the presence of occlusions which often cause inconsistent depth values. To address this issue, we present a novel approach that utilizes a patch-wise cost comparison method to calculate depth. By comparing the 14-point angular cost volume in a patch-wise manner, we ensure that the depth estimator is sensitive to occlusions at the patch level. This enables us to filter out ambiguous matches across different viewing angles and refine the depth estimates within each patch. Furthermore, we employ a patch-based confidence map to weight the final depth estimates, thereby improving overall performance. Experimental results on established datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, with significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness to occlusions. Notably, our approach outperforms existing methods by 2% and 4% on the "4D" and "180" datasets, respectively. Code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/chenyundong/LFDE_OACB. Our approach also achieves state-of-the-art performance on the "4D" dataset, with a depth error of 0.1151, surpassing previous results.
